theme: Real-time and weekly economic indicators: OECD Weekly Tracker (Google Trends based), NY Fed WEI, ONS faster indicators, Dallas Fed mobility, Bundesbank weekly activity index

candidates.name: GoogleTrendsAnchorBank (gtab)
candidates.what_it_holds: Python package `gtab` implementing the anchor-bank calibration method from the CIKM 2020 paper 'Calibration of Google Trends Time Series' (Robert West, EPFL). Directories: gtab/ (core library), example/ (notebooks + CLI demos), cikm2020_paper/ (reproducibility materials). Builds a set of calibration ('anchor') queries so arbitrary Google Trends queries can be placed on one absolute, comparable scale instead of the 0-100 relative index that changes with every pull. Pulls live via pytrends; does not ship pre-built historical data but the anchor-bank building code is a one-command pipeline. MIT license, 217 commits.
candidates.why_useful: Directly targets gap #17 (anchored Google Trends, gtab named explicitly) and gap #4 (point-in-time Google Trends). Our own Trends work failed 0/162 vs naive partly on renormalisation; this is the standard academic fix others (including the OECD Weekly Tracker methodology) build on, so worth testing before concluding Trends is dead.
candidates.last_activity: unknown exact date; 217 commits, actively cited
candidates.time_coverage: user-defined (as far back as Trends allows)
candidates.size_hint: small library, no large data files

candidates.name: trendecon
candidates.what_it_holds: R package that queries Google Trends at multiple frequencies (daily/weekly/monthly) for the same terms and harmonises them into a single consistent daily index, preserving long-run trend levels that a single Trends pull cannot give (Trends caps daily granularity to short windows). Companion site trendecon.org publishes daily-updated Swiss economic indicators built this way. Published in Economic Inquiry (2022). No committed data files -- data pulled on demand via gtrendsR. GPL-3.0, 41 stars, grew out of a 2020 COVID hackathon.
candidates.why_useful: This is essentially a from-scratch, open-source recipe for building an OECD-Weekly-Tracker-style consistent daily/weekly Google Trends series -- addresses the same renormalisation problem that killed our 0/162 Trends test. Could be re-run for US/EMEA travel-adjacent search terms instead of the 9 terms we already tried.
candidates.geography: primarily Switzerland demo; geo parameter is configurable

candidates.name: Opportunity Insights Economic Tracker
candidates.what_it_holds: Full data release behind tracktherecovery.org: county-level, industry- and income-group-cut CSV files in /data (plus a downloadable full-data ZIP), data dictionary (GitHub + PDF), documentation of sources, and a revisions log. Series include consumer spending (from private processors), employment/job postings, and other high-frequency indicators, running from just before COVID to the present with continuing updates (1,892+ commits). Attribution required per series/provider; free to use with citation.
candidates.why_useful: This is the exact repo named in gap #6 (Opportunity Insights Economic Tracker card spend). County-level, high-frequency US consumer spending is a plausible near-term proxy for domestic short-term-rental demand and general consumer strength feeding ABNB's NA segment.
candidates.license: custom (attribution required); data free to use

candidates.name: FRBNY Nowcasting (dynamic factor model)
candidates.what_it_holds: New York Fed's own MATLAB implementation of the dynamic-factor-model nowcasting framework from their Staff Report 830 ('Macroeconomic Nowcasting and Forecasting with Big Data') -- the same family of methodology underlying the NY Fed / now-Dallas-Fed Weekly Economic Index. Ships example US data pulled from FRED, a model-spec template, and a pre-computed DFM results file, but explicitly does NOT include the full proprietary dataset used for the live weekly release (redistribution restricted). BSD-3-Clause, 4 commits visible.
candidates.why_useful: Not a data source, but it is the actual official mixed-frequency DFM code the WEI/GDP nowcast family is built on -- useful if we want to build our own weekly ABNB-demand nowcast (gap #17, MIDAS/DFM nowcasting) rather than only tracking someone else's published index.
candidates.last_activity: unknown exact date; low commit count, appears stable/reference code

candidates.name: nowcast_lstm
candidates.what_it_holds: Python library (with R/MATLAB/Julia wrappers) that packages LSTM neural nets for mixed-frequency economic nowcasting -- handles ragged-edge/missing data common to weekly/monthly indicators, gives ensemble predictions and uncertainty intervals, automatic hyperparameter tuning and feature importance. Ships an example notebook + sample data zip (nowcast_lstm_example.zip). MIT license, 90 commits, actively versioned (v0.2.6).
candidates.why_useful: Same use case as FRBNY Nowcasting but a modern, maintained, easier-to-use alternative for mixed-frequency nowcasting of a weekly/quarterly ABNB demand series from assorted alt-data inputs (gap #17).

candidates.name: nowcastDFM
candidates.what_it_holds: R package implementing dynamic factor models for nowcasting with 'easy estimation and new data contributions to changes in prediction' (attribution decomposition of nowcast updates as new data arrives). 28 stars, from the same author as nowcast_lstm.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative DFM toolkit to FRBNY's MATLAB code, in R, with an explicit feature for decomposing how each new weekly data point moves the nowcast -- useful if building a homegrown weekly ABNB-demand tracker (gap #17).

candidates.name: COVID19_mobility
candidates.what_it_holds: Aggregated mirror of Google, Apple, Waze and TomTom mobility reports during COVID (country/region-level daily mobility change series), committed as data files. 276 stars.
candidates.why_useful: Marginal: covers 2020-2022 mobility only (all four source programs have since been discontinued/archived by their publishers), so it is a historical archive rather than a live indicator, but it is the only committed multi-source mobility mirror found and could still backfill a 2020-22 travel-mobility panel if ever needed for a longer backtest window.

candidates.name: fbi (Factor-Based Imputation) R package
candidates.what_it_holds: R package implementing factor-based missing-data imputation methods (Bai & Ng, Serena Ng lineage) for large macro panels, with a worked vignette using the FRED-MD monthly macro dataset as the demo panel. GPL-3.0, 70 commits.
candidates.why_useful: Could be applied to reconstruct/impute gaps in a weekly or monthly macro panel we assemble (e.g. filling missing weeks in a homemade weekly tracker), tangential fit to point-in-time vintage work (gap #4).
candidates.geography: n/a (generic method); demo uses US FRED-MD

notes: Hard environment constraint: the WebSearch tool returned 'session has used its web search budget (200 of 200)' on the very first query and never recovered for the rest of this scout's run -- this looks like a budget shared across all concurrent scout subagents in this sweep, not specific to this theme, and is worth flagging to whoever is coordinating the sweep since other 'web search' modality scouts running in parallel likely hit the same wall. Fell back to WebFetch on github.com/topics/* pages (worked) and github.com/search?type=repositories (consistently 429 Too Many Requests, retry-after 3600s) plus direct guesses at known repo names from training knowledge. Could NOT find: any GitHub mirror of the OECD Weekly Tracker itself (Woloszko's OECD working paper series appears to publish its index only via OECD.Stat/the OECD website, not a public GitHub repo I could locate), a GitHub mirror of the Dallas Fed Mobility & Engagement Index, a GitHub mirror of the Bundesbank Weekly Activity Index (Bundesbank's own GitHub org has zero public repos), or an ONS 'faster indicators' data repo (ONSdigital's public repos are all software/infrastructure, not the faster-indicators dataset itself -- that series appears to live only on ons.gov.uk). These four named-in-the-brief series are most likely NOT on GitHub at all (published directly by the statistical agency/central bank on their own sites) -- worth noting as a negative finding rather than assuming search failure. What I did find instead, and consider the real value of this pass: (1) two open point-in-time/anchoring fixes for the Google Trends renormalisation problem that killed our own 0/162 test (gtab, trendecon) -- these are worth a second look before fully retiring Trends; (2) the Opportunity Insights Economic Tracker repo itself, named explicitly in gap #6, confirmed live with committed CSVs; (3) the official NY Fed DFM nowcasting code plus two third-party mixed-frequency nowcasting toolkits, which are the actual methodology class behind WEI-style indices, useful if the team wants to build its own weekly ABNB-demand index from inputs already in hand rather than find someone else's finished index. Recommend a follow-up scout specifically hit newyorkfed.org, dallasfed.org, bundesbank.de, and ons.gov.uk directly (not GitHub) for these four named series, since they look native to agency websites, not GitHub-hosted.
